title: The death of Market Street
gist: Noah Smith attributes the collapse of San Francisco's Market Street to three overlapping shocks — a 2019 car ban (that spared buses and trucks), the early-2020s crime wave, and pandemic-driven remote work — and argues the car closure subtracted vehicles while adding no pedestrian space, a mode-of-transit mindset that treated the street as a thoroughfare rather than a destination; despite falling crime and an AI-driven office rebound, foot traffic is still down by half, and he recommends simply re-allowing private cars.

insights.claim: San Francisco's Market Street was destroyed by three compounding factors: the 2019 decision to close the street to cars but not buses, the early-2020s crime wave, and the pandemic-driven shift to remote work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A multi-cause diagnosis matters for asset recovery: fixing only crime or only remote work leaves the policy-induced car ban intact, so downtown SF retail exposure stays impaired.
insights.quote: Cars were subtracted, but pedestrians weren’t added.
insights.locator: In fact, Market Street was destroyed by several things

insights.claim: SF's 20th-century zoning concentrated offices downtown and pushed housing outward, so when workers stopped commuting the downtown emptied out — unlike the mixed-use downtowns of Europe and Asia — and the tech industry's heavy remote-work shift deepened the hit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Single-use downtown zoning is the structural vulnerability behind the 'doom loop,' making mixed-use conversion the durable fix for downtown commercial real estate.
insights.quote: once people stopped going downtown for work, the neighborhood was just a lot more empty, because almost no one lives there
insights.locator: As in many American cities, 20th century urban planning

insights.claim: The 'Doom Loop' is a self-reinforcing cycle: less foot traffic means fewer eyes on the street, more property crime forces store closures, fewer stores cut foot traffic further, and the cycle repeats.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A feedback-loop model implies recovery is nonlinear and requires crossing a threshold before self-reinforcing revival kicks in — key for timing downtown re-entry.
insights.quote: Crime and emptiness fed on each other.
insights.locator: Crime and emptiness fed on each other

insights.claim: American Eagle sued the San Francisco Centre for negligence toward crime, reporting over 100 serious incidents of violence and harassment at its downtown store; the iconic mall then closed in January 2026.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A flagship-tenant lawsuit and anchor-mall closure mark concrete markers of the retail-value destruction that repriced downtown SF commercial property.
insights.quote: American Eagle actually sued the San Francisco Centre for being negligent toward crime, reporting over 100 serious incidents of violence and harassment in its downtown store
insights.locator: The crime wave was another shock

insights.claim: San Francisco property crime fell 27% in 2025 — with burglaries down 29%, larceny (including retail theft) down 22%, and robbery down 24% — and 2026 has seen further drops, making downtown feel materially safer and more orderly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sharp, quantified crime declines remove one leg of the doom loop and are a leading indicator for a downtown retail and real-estate turn.
insights.quote: 2025 alone saw a 27% decrease in property crime, including a 29% decrease in burglaries, a 22% decrease in larceny (including retail theft), and a 24% decrease in robbery
insights.locator: For one thing, crime has begun to fall

insights.claim: The AI boom is driving a modest rebound in San Francisco office-space demand, some office buildings are being converted to housing toward a mixed-use downtown, and both companies and the city are mandating return-to-office.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI-driven office demand plus office-to-housing conversion is the demand-side catalyst for downtown SF commercial real estate, though the author flags it as sluggish.
insights.quote: The AI boom is causing a (modest) rebound in the demand for office space.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the business district is showing

insights.claim: Despite broader recovery signs, Market Street weekday foot traffic remains down by half versus 2019, lagging the rest of downtown.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The persistent 50% foot-traffic gap isolates the car-ban policy effect from the cyclical doom-loop recovery, marking Market Street retail as a distinct impaired pocket.
insights.quote: Weekday foot traffic is still down by half compared to 2019
insights.locator: And yet Market Street remains a dead zone

themes.theme: The car ban that added nothing

insights.claim: Market Street was closed to cars but left open to buses, delivery trucks, and licensed taxis, so it removed parking and Uber/Lyft pickup while a bus can kill a pedestrian as easily as a car — mathematically guaranteeing a less-used street since cars were subtracted but pedestrians never added.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The policy destroyed access without creating pedestrian space, a design failure that explains why the street underperforms and points to what a fix must include.
insights.quote: This mathematically guaranteed that Market Street would become a more empty place: Cars were subtracted, but pedestrians weren’t added.

insights.claim: Even bike traffic on car-free Market Street is considerably lower than pre-pandemic, partly because the promised bike-friendly upgrades never materialized and riders still risk catching tram tracks or being hit by buses and trucks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The car ban failed even on its own pro-bike terms, undercutting the case for mode-restriction policies that don't invest in the intended alternative.
insights.quote: bike traffic on the street is considerably lower than it was pre-pandemic

insights.claim: The $600 million Better Market Street capital project — which promised elevated bike lanes buffering scooters from buses and streetcars — ballooned above a billion dollars before being reined in to $604 million, nearly double the Van Ness Avenue redesign, with the elevated bike lanes scrapped in late 2020 due to SF's lack of state capacity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Chronic cost overruns and scaled-back ambition are a recurring SF state-capacity failure that raises execution risk on any downtown revitalization spend.
insights.quote: The cost of Better Market Street, which soared above a billion dollars before being reined in to a still-staggering $604 million, is almost double the amount spent on the tormented Van Ness Avenue redesign
insights.locator: A $600 million capital project called Better Market Street

insights.claim: SF's urbanists followed a 'bikes and buses good, cars bad' rule that conceives streets as thoroughfares to move people rather than destinations to occupy, contrasting with Paris's Limited Traffic Zone which bans only through-traffic while letting locals drive and reserves real pedestrian areas.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The transit-mode vs. public-space distinction is the reusable lens for evaluating whether a city's car-restriction policy will help or hollow out downtown retail.
insights.quote: Instead of Jane Jacobs, they ended up just being the Robert Moses of buses.
insights.locator: Instead of thinking about how to create spaces

insights.claim: The author's pragmatic recommendation is to simply re-allow private cars on Market Street — not optimal for foot traffic but the quickest fix — noting Mayor Daniel Lurie has already begun by letting certain Uber, Lyft, and Waymo vehicles operate there.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A policy reversal already underway under the current mayor is a concrete near-term catalyst to watch for downtown SF retail access and foot traffic.
insights.quote: Mayor Daniel Lurie has made moves in this direction, allowing certain Uber, Lyft, and Waymo cars to operate on the street
insights.locator: In lieu of turning Market Street into a pedestrian paradise
